channel_name: The Compound and Friends · Josh Brown
video_title: The AI Bubble Already Popped | TCAF 269
gist: Josh Brown, Michael Batnick, Jenny Harrington and Bryn Talkington debate whether the AI bubble already popped (neoclouds, memory and Dell down ~50%, Nvidia shaken by Jensen Huang's exit) on the day of Anthropic's record ~$81B IPO, arguing the broader market is holding up through rotation into HALO/dividend names. Guests pitch Tesla (SpaceX merger thesis), Visa, GPIQ, Cisco, Freeport-McMoRan and Kimberly-Clark, and warn mega-IPOs typically draw down 30-50% in year one.

themes.theme: Did the AI bubble pop? Sentiment vs. activity vs. earnings

insights.claim: Josh Brown argues the AI bubble already popped in July 2026 (about five months before the episode), centered on the neoclouds, which he considered bubbles all along and never owned; Dell, Micron and the RAM ETF have each been cut roughly in half while the Nasdaq sits about 15% off its highs.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: AI hardware drawdowns of ~50% look like a burst bubble even though the index is only modestly off highs.
insights.quote: And the AI bubble already popped in July. We're 5 months into

insights.claim: Panelists distinguish a 'sentiment bubble' from valuation: memory names like Micron traded at single-digit P/Es, so the deflation was in sentiment, not in earnings-unsupported valuations, and stocks cannot rally amid such high skepticism.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Low-multiple AI hardware can still fall when the sentiment premium unwinds; cheap is not a floor.
insights.quote: There's no bubble there. It's just sentiment.

insights.claim: A chart shown on the episode indicated leveraged technology ETF assets collapsed from roughly $130 billion to about $50 billion, cited as evidence the speculative 'activity bubble' has already burst.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Speculative leverage has been flushed, reducing forced-selling fuel from that cohort.
insights.quote: I think it went from like 130 billion to 50 or whatever it was like a total and utter wipeout.

insights.claim: Josh Brown argues money leaving AI is rotating into 'real stocks' people own that aren't AI (the HALO theme), e.g. Coca-Cola up about 40% in 2026, though he concedes defensive names can only go up so much.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: The AI unwind is benefiting non-AI cash-flow names rather than dragging the whole market down.
insights.quote: It's going into real stocks. Stocks that other that people own that aren't AI.

insights.claim: Nvidia authorized an added buyback bringing total authorization to $350 billion, about 9% of its current market cap; Josh Brown says that makes a 'Nvidia to $1 trillion' scenario implausible since executing it would equal taking private a third of the company at that valuation, yet he still would not rush to buy the stock.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Buyback capacity limits downside, but leadership/legal uncertainty argues against bottom-fishing.
insights.quote: I'm telling people I wouldn't rush into this stock and and buy this.

insights.claim: A panelist calls Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia a 'thesis violation', and adds that Anthropic's Dario Amodei reportedly said coding for AMD chips went from six months to three days, which panelists frame as an affront to Nvidia's CUDA moat.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Erosion of CUDA lock-in shifts bargaining power from Nvidia to its customers.
insights.quote: So that's that's CUDA's that's that's that's an affront to CUDA.

insights.claim: Josh Brown argues Nvidia cannot be 're-underwritten' because key questions are unanswerable: whether Jensen Huang or board members knew chips were reaching blacklisted companies in mainland China, how much China revenue survives, how much of the moat was Jensen himself, and how the market will react.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: When thesis inputs are unknowable, standard 'reunderwrite and average down' discipline breaks down.
insights.quote: You can't answer did Jensen Wang or anyone else currently on the board or high ranking have knowledge

insights.claim: Josh Brown says the market is signaling that buyers of compute (frontier model labs like Anthropic) have gained leverage over Nvidia, since they can now spin up AMD server instances in days, something they would not have said publicly while Jensen controlled global GPU supply.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Pricing power in AI may migrate from chip suppliers to model companies.
insights.quote: The market is telling me that it believes that the buyers of compute have gained maybe not the upper hand, but have gained hand.

insights.claim: A co-host notes that in hindsight the market was sober about Nvidia, which traded at about 12x forward earnings versus roughly 20x for the market despite ~70% earnings growth, while memory stocks were rich despite ~3x forward P/Es; DRAM is down 52%, and Micron never got past 10x earnings, evidence of discernment and skepticism shaped by circular-financing worries.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Cyclical peak earnings make low P/Es misleading; the market priced AI hardware as cyclical.

insights.claim: Panelists frame the key open question as whether there was an 'earnings bubble': AI company earnings (e.g., Google Cloud growth of 98% year-over-year) cannot keep growing at that pace, so the market derated those stocks on unsustainable future earnings.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Derating reflects doubt about the durability of hypergrowth rather than current earnings.
insights.quote: were we in an earnings bubble?

insights.claim: Panelists argue a slowdown in hyperscaler capex could be bullish: if the Magnificent 7 (about 38% of the market) return to less cash bleed or positive free cash flow, the market would be majorly stabilized; Anthropic's IPO also shows the capex is 'money good' with public capital while OpenAI must still go to private capital.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Less AI capex could re-rate mega-caps on free cash flow recovery.
insights.quote: If Google and Meta Cash cash flow starts turning back up, the market's going to love it.

insights.claim: Josh Brown says what saved the market after the Democrats' midterm clean sweep (with data centers a top exit-poll issue) was the realization that the hyperscalers already own the compute, making it more valuable if supply is constrained, and that the Street's refusal to reward capex hikes would push them back to positive cash flow sooner; Alphabet rallied.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Political limits on data-center buildouts can raise the value of existing compute holders.
insights.quote: these are the companies that have the compute. So if we think there's going to be less of it than expected that compute is worth more.

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington cites seasonality that from November to the end of June after midterms the S&P has been up every time since 1942 (she says '21 out of 20 times'), averaging about 16%, because the election is a clearing event.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Post-midterm seasonality is a tailwind into mid-2027.

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington calls Fed Governor Waller's repeated calls for an immediate 50 basis point rate hike 'insane' and nonsensical.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Hawkish Fed rhetoric is a live macro headwind she dismisses.
insights.quote: For some reason, he needs to tell everyone we need a 50 basis point hike immediately. I think that's insane.

insights.claim: Panelists suggest a cycle with a third-or-fourth-inning bubble deflation, followed by recalibration, is preferable to another 100% Nasdaq run, and that repeated shocks (Liberation Day, the war) may have let air out of the balloon and made the market more resilient.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: An early partial deflation could extend the AI cycle rather than end it.

themes.theme: Anthropic IPO, LLM competition and AI routing

insights.claim: Anthropic's IPO raised about $81 billion (largest US-listed IPO by deal size, ahead of SpaceX at ~$75 billion and SK Hynix at $26.5 billion, a redomicile), priced at $83 and traded around $97 on day one; Josh Brown bought it and argues a truly burst bubble would have left it a flop near $70.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Strong demand for a mega AI IPO undercuts the 'everything AI is broken' narrative.
insights.quote: would Anthropic who priced at 83 be trading at 97 right now?

insights.claim: Anthropic's count of customers spending $100,000 or more grew from about 1,500 in December 2025 to 11,900 by September 2026, which a co-host says answers earlier doubts about monetization; the company only started making money in March 2023.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI demand is real and accelerating, supporting model-company revenue.
insights.quote: it went to 11,900 from 1500 spending six figures to 11,900 in a year. The demand is unbelievable.

insights.claim: Panelists expect multiple LLM winners (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini) for at least the next few years rather than winner-take-all like Google search, with enterprises flipping between or using all three, though the 5-10 year end state is opaque.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Avoid betting on a single model winner near term.
insights.quote: I think it's going to be multiple players for at least the next few years

insights.claim: Josh Brown says Google's installed base (around 11 apps with a billion users each) makes it a formidable gateway to push Gemini into Gmail, Docs, Sheets and YouTube regardless of user preference; Apple has similar distribution power but chooses not to use it.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Distribution may matter more than model quality in consumer AI.
insights.quote: They have, I think, 11 apps with a billion users each

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington argues frontier labs are all building Ferraris while most LLM users need a CR-V, implying overinvestment in top-end models relative to typical use cases.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Mass-market AI demand may favor cheaper, good-enough models, pressuring frontier economics.
insights.quote: everyone's in this race to build a Ferrari. And the reality is is most of the people who are going to use LLMs, like they need a CRV

insights.claim: Panelists say auto-routing tools (Microsoft's Copilot/co-work 'auto' mode choosing among Opus, OpenAI and others; Perplexity's neutral model picker) and agent harnesses will route simpler tasks to cheaper models, which is how enterprise AI spend will be used effectively.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Model commoditization via routing could compress per-query pricing for frontier labs.
insights.quote: the harness is going to decide what to route where.

insights.claim: Josh Brown wishes Anthropic had come public at $500 billion rather than about $1.8 trillion, warning politicians will weaponize the valuation as 'dumping on retail'; Rep. Pramila Jayapal criticized the IPO over outages and security risks, which Jenny Harrington dismissed as anti-capitalist pandering.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: High IPO valuations invite political backlash and regulatory headline risk.
insights.quote: I just wish it came public at 500 billion

themes.theme: Mega-IPOs, private-market excess and retail access

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington warns that newly IPO'd companies historically suffer first-year drawdowns of 30-50%: SpaceX and SK Hynix fell ~50%, Alibaba ~50%, Visa 36% (2008), Rivian 90%, with Mastercard the rare exception; investors should use those drawdowns to buy.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Be patient with Anthropic and other mega-IPOs; better entry points likely come within a year.
insights.quote: investors need to understand the first year a company IPOs has a really long history of draw downs of 30 to 50% at some point. So take advantage of that.

insights.claim: Of the largest recent IPOs, nearly all are down from highs, including CoreWeave -62%, Lineage -48% and Cerebras -52%; SpaceX priced at $135, opened near $175, peaked around $225 and fell to roughly $105-107.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Don't buy on the opening print of hot IPOs.
insights.quote: the moral of the story is don't buy on the opening.

insights.claim: Josh Brown counters bears by noting the market digested the three largest IPOs ever inside one year and they trade above their offer prices, though he concedes the 'market can't absorb all the supply' bear case may be playing out.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Equity supply absorption is a key watch item for the bull case.
insights.quote: are you not impressed by the fact that we just digested three of the largest IPOs of all the three numbers one, two, and three inside of one year

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington argues post-Sarbanes-Oxley/Reg FD regulation and VC growth keep companies like Stripe private so long that the juice is squeezed out before IPO, so late-stage IPOs like a $2 trillion SpaceX have a lot priced in.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Public investors get late-stage, fully priced companies; expect weaker post-IPO returns.
insights.quote: So I think when you have SpaceX at 2 trillion IPO, it's a lot priced in.

insights.claim: Josh Brown says the Trump-era culture lets Wall Street promote IPOs unabashedly (Jamie Dimon on stage with Dario Amodei for Anthropic's roadshow, Morgan Stanley setting up a theme park for SpaceX), and retail now gets large allocations (about 20% of Anthropic) because compliance fears that kept retail out have loosened in the Robinhood era.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Heavy retail allocations in hot IPOs raise the risk of sentiment-driven post-IPO volatility.
insights.quote: Wall Street is not ashamed or embarrassed at all to be promoting these equities in a way that we've never seen.

insights.claim: Michael Batnick uses Robinhood as a template: it IPO'd at roughly $20-30 billion in 2021, fell below $10 billion (-75%+), and five years later is a $60 billion real business; he says there is no way Kalshi, reportedly raising at $60-65 billion, is worth as much as Robinhood, especially after Michigan ordered it to shut down gambling and return client funds within 30 days.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Private growth-equity marks (e.g., Kalshi) look inflated relative to public comps.
insights.quote: There is no way in real life that Khi is worth as much or more than Robin Hood.

insights.claim: A panelist argues private-market firms resist IPOs because a public listing forces mark-to-market on comparable holdings, which could expose valuations far below book marks and crack the private ecosystem.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: IPO scarcity partly reflects fear of revealing stale private marks.

themes.theme: Rotation, market structure and the 'Berkshire market'

insights.claim: Michael Batnick notes Nvidia lost over $2 trillion in market cap in about 30 days while the market hung near all-time highs, arguing market-cap weighting self-corrects and that the claim the whole market was propped up by AI has been demonstrably false so far.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Index resilience amid mega-cap tech collapse argues against calls to abandon cap-weighting.
insights.quote: what's been proven to not be true is that the entire market was being propped up by AI demonstrabably false at this point.

insights.claim: In March, when the Strait of Hormuz was closed, nearly every sector fell; in the current selloff real estate, utilities, staples and energy held up, and Michael Batnick calls such rotation the lifeblood of a bull market, while the spread between tech/semis average drawdown and the cap-weighted index has never been higher.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Broad sector participation suggests an intact bull market despite AI weakness.
insights.quote: And this is the lifeblood of a bull market as rotation.

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington says the equal-weight S&P (RSP) hit an all-time high just last week, echoing 2000 when excluding tech you did very well.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Equal-weight/ex-tech exposure is the 2000-style playbook working now.
insights.quote: Cuz RSP was just at an all-time high, I think, last week.

insights.claim: A dot-com chart shows tech and communication services fell 69% while the rest of the market was flat to slightly up peak-to-trough, the so-called 'Berkshire market' of housing, retail and non-internet companies, which Josh Brown likens to today's HALO trade.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for non-tech outperformance during a tech bust.
insights.quote: Berkshire market, we used to call it flat.

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington says broad dividend stocks were 10%+ ahead of the market in Q1 2026, ~3% ahead in Q2, behind in Q3, and are now about 8% ahead, while small caps have been killed this year; she says rotation is better viewed by strategy than by sector.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Dividend/value strategies are having a strong but highly volatile relative year.
insights.quote: broadly dividend stocks ended the first quarter like 10 plus percent ahead of the market.

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington describes intraday rotation so violent that her dividend strategy started the day ~2% behind as Kimberly-Clark and Clorox fell while semis rallied, then finished 25-30 basis points ahead, calling it pure blind basket rotation.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Daily factor swings create noise and entry opportunities in defensives.
insights.quote: it's just pure blind stupid rotation

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington argues market structure has fundamentally changed for the worse, with algorithmic and hedge-fund pair trades reacting to tweets, magnified by concentrated sector indexes (e.g., Eli Lilly and J&J about 40% of healthcare).
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Index concentration plus algos amplify single-stock moves into sector moves.

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington says dogmatic value managers during the dot-com bubble (Jeremy Grantham, Gary Brinson) were right but lost clients who couldn't stay along for the ride.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Being early and dogmatic is commercially indistinguishable from being wrong.

themes.theme: Value discipline and the memory/old-tech round trip

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington cites Bruce Greenwald's value principle that if you loved a stock at 50 you should love it more at 40, framed today as 're-underwriting' the thesis, with the starting point always being today.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Re-evaluate theses on price declines rather than anchoring to past prices.
insights.quote: if you loved it at 50 you should love it more at 40

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington's discipline growth strategy requires a 5% or better free cash flow yield, so Meta was the only AI-adjacent mega-cap that qualified; Nvidia and Google were rejected over earnings risk and stock-option dilution, and SanDisk at ~3x earnings lacked free cash flow yield.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: An FCF-yield screen kept her out of the memory/AI hardware blowup.
insights.quote: the discipline growth strategy has a 5% or better free cash flow yield on it. So, that's why that's why um Meta was the only one that made it in.

insights.claim: SanDisk, Seagate and Western Digital were all held in Jenny Harrington's dividend strategy within the past decade (she bought memory coming out of the pandemic when it traded as if it had no value), and old-tech names like Dell, Cisco, HP, Ciena and Western Digital became momentum stocks again in the AI buildout.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Memory and old hardware remain cyclical commodities; momentum phases revert.
insights.quote: memory was trading as if it had no value.

themes.theme: Stock picks: Halo, income and copper

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington owns Tesla and predicts it will become a subsidiary of SpaceX within three years, citing new synergies in energy and robotics (Megapacks, robots, Colossus) per Elon Musk's recent comments; she thinks Tesla holders would need a large premium to accept.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: A SpaceX-Tesla combination would be a major catalyst for Tesla shareholders.
insights.quote: This will be a subsidiary of SpaceX within the next three years.

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington likes Visa as a duopoly with ~60-62% margins (down from 66%), noting crypto failed to disrupt it and that a proposed credit-card interest-rate cap from Elizabeth Warren would hit lenders like Capital One, not Visa or Mastercard, which only process swipes.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Rate-cap headline risk is misapplied to the networks; Visa is a compounding bet on consumer spending.
insights.quote: They're just the rails. They're just the rails. They're just the swipes.

insights.claim: Bryn Talkington recommends GPIQ, Goldman's Nasdaq-100 covered-call ETF, which writes at-the-money calls on 20-50% of the portfolio targeting ~10.5% income, currently only ~25% covered (leaving 75% upside exposure), with most distributions classified as return of capital for tax efficiency.
insights.speaker: Bryn Talkington
insights.so_what: Tax-efficient covered-call income with flexible upside participation keeps clients invested through cycles.
insights.quote: The majority of the covered call premium is return of capital.

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington likes Cisco after 40% earnings growth last quarter, a 5% free cash flow yield and 17x multiple, expecting double-digit earnings growth for three years because AI complexity rests on the network regardless of which chip or memory maker wins.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: A picks-and-shovels AI play that is agnostic to the chip winner, at a value multiple.
insights.quote: It doesn't matter who's making the chips. It doesn't matter who's got the memory.

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington likes Freeport-McMoRan at a 7% free cash flow yield and 13x earnings, down 26% from its August high, citing endless copper demand (EVs ~35 lbs of copper vs ~4 lbs for ICE cars) and tight supply from Chilean mine issues; Josh Brown objects the stock is in free fall, and Bryn Talkington wants the technicals to stop falling first.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Copper fundamentals look strong but price momentum argues for patience on entry.
insights.quote: An electric car has like 35 lbs of copper in it.

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington calls Kimberly-Clark 'Halo 101': a 4.5% dividend yield, 54 straight years of dividends, 15.5x earnings, and a Kenvue combination expected to yield $2 billion in synergies lifting earnings growth to high single digits; she thinks it could double over five years.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Merger synergies can turn a sleepy staple into a total-return compounder.
insights.quote: It's got a 4 and a.5% dividend yield.

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington's hurdle rate: any equity held for at least five years should be expected to double, with roughly a quarter of that return from dividends for a name like Kimberly-Clark.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: A concrete hurdle (≈15% annualized) for vetting long-term holdings.
insights.quote: that should be your expectation or you're buying the wrong stocks

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington won an April 9 bet with Josh Brown when Netflix and Disney were both at $100: Disney has reached about $120 while Netflix fell to about $58; she attributes Josh's miss to how hard AI is coming for content creation and notes Disney fits HALO with the high-end consumer and ESPN growth holding.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: AI-driven content disruption is a risk to pure streaming relative to diversified media assets.
insights.quote: what you missed I think on Netflix was how hard AI was coming for um the content creation

insights.claim: Jenny Harrington says she lost her Nvidia-vs-Intel bet with Josh Brown because she underestimated how badly Intel's management could destroy a company despite expected cash flows.
insights.speaker: Jenny Harrington
insights.so_what: Management quality can override cheap cash-flow-based theses.
insights.quote: how much management could really destroy a company.
